name: Aminata Diallo
headline: 19-year-old apprentice bricklayer and part-time student, Bamako, Mali
description: Aminata Diallo rises before dawn each day, the only light in her rented room the thin glow of a kerosene lamp. She lives in a bustling district on the outskirts of Bamako, where the walls are packed earth and the roof corrugated tin. There is no tap; she fills a bucket each morning at the communal stand two blocks away, carrying it back with a careful, balanced gait that avoids splashing her only pair of work trousers. She wears them six days a week to the construction site, where she is the youngest person on the crew and the only woman. Her master mason, an old man named Sékou who lost two fingers to a faulty crane, calls her la petite comptable because she recalculates every load-bearing estimate in her head before she lifts a trowel. She does not laugh at his teasing; she simply nods and checks the angle of the plumb line again. Double-checking is not a habit she learned from a textbook—it is a reflex born from watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Aminata was twelve when her mother died, and she has been counting everything ever since: the number of bricks in a pallet, the cost of a bag of rice, the weeks until her next accounting exam. She keeps a small notebook tucked inside her shirt, its pages filled with figures and dates, and under the loosest floorboard near her mattress she hides an emergency fund—exactly the same amount each month, never touched, never counted in daylight. At night, after ten hours of hauling cement and stacking blocks, she studies by the lamp until her eyes burn. The accounting course she is saving for meets at a community center on the other side of the city, but she cannot afford the bus fare both ways, so she walks. She walks past the stalls of women selling fried plantains, past the boys who whistle and call her mademoiselle bâtisseuse, and she keeps her eyes on the ground, counting her steps. She is saving for something else too, something she does not write in her notebook: a proper room with running water, where her younger sister can come live with her and go to school. But she does not speak of this aloud, because in her experience, plans that are spoken become plans that are borrowed against. Her coworkers respect her silence, her precision, the way she never asks for an advance on her wage. They do not know that she once watched her father sell his tools to pay for a funeral and never held a trowel again. Aminata holds hers every day, and she checks every measurement twice, because she has learned that the only thing you can trust is what you have counted yourself.
